column1: # Files malware leaves on disk. One line each, tab separated. After editing, run: bash tools/gen.sh
#   incident  an id from data/incidents.tsv
#   os        all, mac, linux or win (win is Git Bash and gird-check.ps1)
#   kind      wiper    a file of gh-token-monitor (its path must name it), the wiper that runs a destructive command when a
#                      stolen GitHub token is revoked. Section 5 tells people to stop it first.
#             startup  a file that starts malware at login, or the malware such a file starts, or a copy of
#                      malware that hooks it adds to an agent run at each session; the note is shown under it.
#                      A Python incident's (data/bad-pypi.tsv) is shown in that incident's row, never as npm
#                      malware, and must be in the home folder (~) with owner no
#             site     a file in any Python environment's site-packages: a Python incident's hit
#             temp     an entry in /tmp, TMPDIR or %TEMP%: a Python incident's hit. May end in *
#   owner     yes: counts only if this person owns it (for files in the shared /tmp; %TEMP% on Windows is the
#             person's own folder, so there it always counts). no otherwise
#   path      wiper and startup: a file or folder, with the path tokens data/sessions.tsv uses, an
#             absolute path, or {PROGRAMDATA} (Windows' ProgramData). site and temp: a file name
#   note      startup: what the file does, as shown under it. temp: what to do about the files, from the
#             incident's advisory, shown under the incident's row when they are found (the temp lines of one
#             incident carry the same note). - for wiper and site
# gh-token-monitor: Wiz (TanStack wave: the LaunchAgent and the systemd unit), Socket (keyv wave: the
# first six) and Tensorlake's own advisory, GHSA-8g63-53c9-65j2 (the LaunchAgent, the systemd unit,
# ~/.config/gh-token-monitor and ~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh, and on Windows the gh-token-monitor
# folder in %LOCALAPPDATA% and a scheduled task named gh-token-monitor, both to delete). All seven carry
# the tanstack id, though the two /tmp logs come only from Socket's keyv post and the Windows folder only
# from Tensorlake's: the report and fleet mode name a wiper line as gh-token-monitor, never as its
# incident.
# Mastra: Socket, whose protocal.cjs is the implant itself, which its LaunchAgent, its systemd unit and,
# on Windows, a Run key start at login. It also names the implant's config
# (~/.config/NodePackages/config.json on Linux, a config.json beside protocal.cjs on Windows) and the
# loader's temp markers, .pkg_history and .pkg_logs:
# no kind fits them, since a config starts nothing and a temp line is a Python incident's hit (it gives
# its incident a Python row in section 5), so they have no line.
# mistralai: its advisory, which lists the file and a process started through it as signs.
# guardrails-ai 0.10.1: SafeDep's post on the TanStack wave, whose code recovered from it writes the same
# /tmp/transformers.pyz on Linux and runs it; its note is the maintainer's advice (GHSA-xmpw-2vmm-p4p6). A
# temp file the lines of two Python incidents name is listed once: with the first of them whose package
# was found (in a Python environment or uv's cache), so a hit never names a package that is not there,
# else with the first of them, as written by either.
# LiteLLM: its advisory, and the GitHub issue the advisory links for the attack's details
# (BerriAI/litellm#47826), which names the .pc_ temp files and PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE: the .pc_once_ marker is
# written only once the data was sent, the advisory's "the exfil is confirmed".
# LiteLLM 1.82.7 and 1.82.8: LiteLLM's March post, which says to look for litellm_init.pth in
# site-packages and remove it (1.82.8). And ~/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py, the backdoor its payload writes:
# Wiz says the payload uses the persistence of the KICS attack, whose post names ~/.config/sysmon and
# sysmon.py on a Linux host; HuskyHacks' teardown of 1.82.8 shows the code that writes the file and a
# systemd user service, sysmon.service, to start it; NovaSky's hunt saw the file written on an affected
# host. HuskyHacks finds the write fails on a machine with no Kubernetes service account token, so a
# missing file proves nothing. Its os is all, though the sources describe Linux hosts: the code HuskyHacks
# shows runs that write with no check of the system, and creates the folder and opens the file before
# the line that fails, so a payload that ran without the token, on a Mac too, can leave an empty
# sysmon.py. The service has no line: monitoring tools can use that name.
# AntV wave: SafeDep, which names the kitty-monitor backdoor's systemd unit and LaunchAgent, the cat.py
# they start at login, and the payload copies in ~/.claude/package and ~/.codex/package that the
# SessionStart hooks it adds to Claude Code and Codex settings run. Its /var/tmp/.gh_update_state, the
# backdoor's state file, has no line: a temp line is a Python incident's hit in /tmp, TMPDIR or %TEMP%,
# and a wiper path must name gh-token-monitor. Its ~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh is a wiper line.
# Nx Console 18.95.0, the AntV wave's extension: Nx's own advisory (GHSA-c9j4-9m59-847w) and postmortem
# name the same cat.py and LaunchAgent. A file an npm incident's line and an editor extension
# incident's line both name is listed once: with the extension when that extension was found and none
# of the npm incident's packages were, else as npm malware. Its /var/tmp/.gh_update_state, /tmp/kitty-*
# and their %TEMP% copies have no line, as for the AntV wave, nor %USERPROFILE%\.bun\bin\bun.exe, where
# Bun's own installer puts Bun.
# durabletask 1.4.1 to 1.4.3: Wiz's post on it, which names /tmp/managed.pyz, the payload it downloads (as
# GitHub's malware advisory does). Not its /tmp/rope-*.pyz (a temp line's * may only end the name), its
# /tmp/.rope_state folder (a temp line in the shared /tmp counts a file this person owns under one name,
# never a folder), its ~/.cache/.sys-update-check markers (no kind fits a marker in the home folder: it
# starts nothing, and a temp line is in the temp folder), nor its systemd unit, pgsql-monitor.service,
# whose folder no source gives and whose name monitoring tools can use.
# telnyx 4.87.2: Telnyx's own advisory, which names ~/.config/audiomon/audiomon.py (Linux and macOS),
# the systemd unit that starts it (Linux), /tmp/.initd_state (Linux and macOS) and msbuild.exe in the
# Startup folder (Windows, %APPDATA%; a Python incident's startup file is under ~, so its line takes
# the usual ~/AppData/Roaming). Its msbuild.exe.lock has no line: the advisory gives no folder for it.
# GlassWorm's LaunchAgent: Socket. A startup file of an incident whose packages are only editor
# extensions (data/bad-extensions.tsv) is shown with them, as that incident's sign, not as npm malware,
# and only when an extension that shipped malware is found: alone, it is a file to check.
# incident
